tagline.text: A January festival in Ilagan that honors Isabela's harvest with scarecrows

location.label: Location
location.text: Ilagan City, Isabela (around the Provincial Capitol complex and Isabela Sports Complex)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000~8,000 (round-trip transport from Manila, 1 night's lodging and meals, rough estimate per person)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Cauayan Airport (CYZ) or Tuguegarao Airport (TUG); overland from Manila (MNL) is also possible

children.text: The Bambanti Festival is the biggest annual festival of Isabela province, held every January in the capital, Ilagan. Built around the scarecrow, called bambanti in Ilocano, it celebrates a bountiful harvest with a Bambanti Village exhibition, street dancing and cooking contests.

The Bambanti Festival is held every January by Isabela province in the Cagayan Valley region of northern Luzon. Bambanti is the Ilocano word for scarecrow, a symbol that protects farmers in a region built around corn and tobacco. The provincial government calls it the "mother of all festivals" because it honors residents' way of life, history and heritage. The main stage is the provincial capital, Ilagan City, and the main venues are the Provincial Capitol complex and the Isabela Sports Complex.

The festival is said to have begun in 1997 under then-governor Benjamin Dy. It was not held from 2005 to 2010, was revived in 2011 when it moved to January, and was skipped again in 2021 and 2022 during the pandemic. It won the Best Festival Practices award at the Aliw Awards for 2015–2017, and in 2019 it was recognized by Guinness World Records for the most people dressed and dancing as scarecrows. The record group is reported as 2,495 dancers.

The festival changes a little every year. In 2025 it ran from January 19 to 25, and the provincial government said more than 250,000 people had attended the year before. That year's theme was "the festival of the new Philippines," with an emphasis on inclusion built into each event, and 38 diplomats from 24 countries joined a trade forum and tour. Dates and programs are set each year, so check the latest notices from the Isabela provincial government and the Ilagan City tourism office before you go.

For travelers, this festival is a chance to see northern Luzon's rural culture in one place. Each city and town builds a pavilion from local materials such as bamboo, corn, shells and mung beans, and the day is made of shopping for local products and food, followed by a concert in the evening. Because Ilagan is far from Manila, plan at least one night, and it is safer to book lodging early. Within Ilagan you can get between venues by tricycle, so grouping a few main spots into each day makes the plan much easier.

Isabela's cities and towns set up booths in the Provincial Capitol complex. The pavilions are built from local materials such as bamboo, corn, shells and mung beans, with local products and tourist attractions on display, so you can tour the whole province in one place. In 2025 there were 34 booths with lit-up giant scarecrow installations. Booth staff will sometimes explain local travel information in person, which helps when planning your next trip.

blocks.title: Street dancing and festival dance showdown

children.text: This is the highlight of the festival. Contingents from each city and town dance in the streets in colorful scarecrow-style costumes and then compete in the finals at the Isabela Sports Complex. In 2025, 13 teams reached the finals and Ilagan City won the overall title. The stadium is said to hold up to 40,000 people. Most costumes and props take their inspiration from farm tools and grain, so the joy of harvest shows in the dance moves too.

blocks.title: The scarecrow dance that set a Guinness record

children.text: In 2019, 2,495 dancers in scarecrow costumes were recognized as a Guinness record. A crowd that size is not seen every year, but it is worth knowing as the moment the scarecrow costume became a symbol of the festival.

blocks.title: Festival King and Queen costume contest

children.text: Representatives of each city and town show off lavish costumes inspired by scarecrows and rural themes. In 2025, 13 cities and towns took part, and the costumes were reportedly shown in advance at a shopping mall.
A beauty pageant in which contestants wear gowns made from inabel, the local woven textile. In 2025 it was held at the Capital Arena in Ilagan City.
A cooking contest for local food and drinks. One year the theme was Isabela longganisa (sausage), and Tumauini's blood sausage is said to have taken first place. In 2025, 22 teams took part.

At Queen Isabela Park there were acoustic, band and hip-hop shows each evening, and the last night featured a grand concert with well-known singers. The lineup changes every year, so check the notices on site.
Isabela is an agricultural province known for corn and tobacco. At the festival booths you can buy local food and handicrafts, and scarecrow decoration items are sold too.

items.title: 2-day, 1-night course
items.subtitle: Exhibits by day, performances by night in Ilagan

children.text: Take a long-distance bus from Manila toward Ilagan. Travel time varies a lot with traffic, so check at the terminal.
Arrive in Ilagan and drop your bags at your lodging. Rooms fill up early during festival week.
Take a slow walk through Bambanti Village in the Provincial Capitol complex. Compare the different materials and scarecrow installations from each city and town.
After dinner, watch the night show at Queen Isabela Park.
On the second morning, find a spot to watch the street dancing. The date of the finals differs each year, so check the local schedule.
When the events are over, head to the terminal in time for your bus home.

Even though the midday sun in January is mild, outdoor events run long. Bring a hat, water and a thin layer to wear over your clothes. On the second morning you can stop by the city market and pick up local food such as longganisa as a keepsake. Buses home fill up on the final day of the festival, so get a ticket for an early departure if you can.

items.title: Same-day local course
items.subtitle: If you are coming from a nearby city

children.text: Arrive in central Ilagan and start with Bambanti Village.
Try Isabela longganisa at a cooking-contest booth or a restaurant in town.
Move to the venue of the street dancing or costume contest and watch.
Head back quickly before the crowds leave.
The venues are a bit far to walk between, so most people use a tricycle. Fares depend on distance, so negotiate before you get in.
A long-distance bus is the most common way to get from Manila to Ilagan. Several bus companies serve Isabela, and travel time and fares vary by company and traffic, so check at the terminal.
During the festival, seats fill up quickly, so it helps to line up both your outbound and return tickets in advance.
If you drive, head toward the North Luzon Expressway; on festival days parking in central Ilagan is difficult.
Flights from Manila toward Tuguegarao or Cauayan operate at certain times, but routes change, so check the latest timetable.
From the airport to Ilagan, use a van, a bus or a rental car. Check fares and travel time on site.
In Ilagan, tricycles are the basic means of transport. Traffic around venues may be controlled, so follow the instructions.
The venues are spread apart, so it is more efficient to group the main places into each day.

The Bambanti Festival is held in late January. In 2018 it ran from January 22 to 28, in 2024 it started on January 22, and in 2025 it ran from January 19 to 25. The exact dates change every year, so be sure to confirm the schedule.
If you visit Ilagan at any other time, you will not see the festival displays. The winter months, when the dry season begins, are relatively cool and good for outdoor events.

Even after the festival, the countryside in Isabela changes with the corn and tobacco harvest, so a trip just for the rural scenery is possible too. The scarecrow displays and parades, however, can be seen only during festival week.

rows: Festival period. Mornings and evenings are cool.
Sun protection is needed for outdoor activities at midday.
Northern Luzon can lie in a typhoon path, so check your plans.

There are hotels and guesthouses in Ilagan and in nearby Cauayan City, and rooms run out early during festival week. If possible, book about two months ahead to be safe. Facilities and rates differ by property, so check recent reviews.

The signature food is Isabela longganisa (sausage), which is often the theme of the cooking contest. Local snacks such as inatata and bala-bala have also been featured as festival foods. Each booth tastes different, so try a little at several.

Alternating between market stall food and restaurants in town keeps costs down. Festival markets sell many freshly grilled or fried snacks, so rather than buying a lot at once, share and graze as you walk around. For drinks with water or ice, check the hygiene with your own eyes before choosing. If you cannot find lodging, you can stay in a nearby city and travel in the morning, but keep in mind the longer travel time if you need to match event times.
Check the schedule in the notices of the Isabela provincial government or the Ilagan City tourism office before you go.
The street dancing finals draw large crowds, so arrive early and claim a shaded spot.
Bambanti Village photographs better around dusk, when the lights come on, than in the daytime.
Bring plenty of cash. Market stalls and tricycles generally take cash only.
Because Ilagan is far from Manila, book your round-trip transport in advance.
Evening venues are crowded, so keep your belongings in front of you and look after valuables.
The scarecrow costumes carry local feeling, so ask first before taking photos.
It is very loud near the stage, so bring earplugs if you have children with you.
Each city and town booth exists to promote the area, so you can pick up brochures. Use it as a chance to gather information for your next trip.
Besides Tagalog, Ilocano is widely spoken locally. Learning a few simple greetings will please vendors.
Event schedules and locations change every year, and northern Luzon can be hit by typhoons in the rainy season.
Check the provincial government's notices for the latest schedule and traffic controls.
Some events may require advance registration or have controlled areas.
Watch out for pickpockets at crowded events.
If a typhoon forecast is issued, adjust your plans.
Because it is a long trip from Manila, leave extra time for your bus home.
Even in January, outside the rainy season, it can rain suddenly during events, so bring a light raincoat.

A commercial city near Ilagan with many hotels and restaurants, so it is a candidate when you look for lodging. Check the distance and travel time on site. If you need cash, find out where the ATMs are in Ilagan or Cauayan beforehand.
The site where Bambanti Village is built; during the festival this area is the center.
The venue for evening shows and the costume contest, and a good place to visit at night.
